source.title: Demystifying Synthetic Data in LLM Pre-training: A Systematic Study of Scaling Laws, Benefits, and Pitfalls
source.authors: Fei-Yang Kang; Newsha Ardalani; Michael Kuchnik; Youssef Emad; Mostafa Elhoushi; Shubhabrata Sengupta; Shang-Wen Li; Ramya Raghavendra; Ruo-Xi Jia; Carole-Jean Wu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits and validates power-law-style loss scaling relations using its own training runs, testing scaling predictability in synthetic and natural-data settings with a different experimental scope.
record.gate_note: The paper tests data and model scaling, but does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its mixture-ratio, generator-size, and unigram analyses are not separate rows for these claim versions. Scaling-law results cited from other work are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The study fits saturating power laws (L = B/D^β + E; L = A/N^α + E) to its own pretraining runs on natural, synthetic and mixed text. It checks them on held-out larger runs. This tests V1, and V2 only weakly, in a new setting: synthetic-data mixtures. Scaling laws are mainly its tool for comparing data mixtures, but it does report its own fit-validation results, so it is not T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The paper's main conclusions concern synthetic data: mixing about 30% rephrased text with web text speeds convergence 5–10x and lowers projected irreducible loss. Pure rephrased data is not better than CC, and textbook data hurts. Good ratios depend on scale, and generators larger than about 8B do not help. The scaling fits are presented as validated tools, and the authors flag frontier-scale validation as future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses power-law-style relations with additive irreducible-loss terms for data scaling, model scaling, and a joint model/data fit; tests mixtures of natural and synthetic text in Llama-3-based models trained from scratch.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported loss outcomes vary with synthetic-data type and mixture ratio, and the relative results differ between data-scaling and model-scaling analyses. The paper also reports that preferred mixture ratios vary with model size and data budget.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The reported validation checks extend only to 200B tokens and 3B parameters; larger-scale curves are extrapolations rather than observations. Aggregate fit errors are reported without per-mixture errors or uncertainty estimates. The paper notes that its experiments reach 3B parameters and 200B tokens, below frontier scales.
record.rows_left_out: The text reports qualitative mixture-comparison findings and additional loss-curve details in Figures 1 and 2, but does not provide per-mixture numerical curve values in the text. These were not transcribed as separate rows; the aggregate fit-validation errors and the stated large-scale forecasts are recorded in R1–R4.

untested.parts: Compute as the varied axis. Model scaling at data budgets other than 50B tokens. Scales beyond 3B parameters and 200B tokens.
Extrapolation by orders of magnitude: validation covers only 2x in data and 1.5x in parameters. The 8T-token and 400B-parameter forecasts are unverified.
Not tested. A joint L(N,D) fit exists, but no compute-optimal split is derived or tested.
Not tested. Shapes are fixed per size (Table 1).
Not tested. The study covers text pretraining only, with no other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Not tested. Only loss is measured, and the authors list no NLP benchmarks as a limitation.
Fitting-method, schedule and parameter-counting sensitivity are not tested. Fitted exponents per mixture are not reported numerically.

missing.what: Per-mixture estimates of irreducible loss E from the joint fit L(N,D)=A/N^α+B/D^β+E. All synthetic mixtures except pure QA have lower E than CC, and 33% HQ+67% CC is lowest.
Qualitative evidence that the relative ranking of mixtures differs between data-scaling and model-scaling fits. For example, the 67% versus 33% rephrased ratio flips.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The reader's V2 limits_scope label on R3/R4 was removed: unverified forecasts are untested parts, not limits. V2 support is weak because validation spans at most 2x. Uncertainty is not reported, and per-mixture errors and exponents are not given in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests data scaling at a fixed 1B parameter count and model scaling at a fixed 50B-token budget. It does not test scaling with compute as the varied axis, nor establish behavior across several orders of magnitude in frontier-scale runs.
It validates predictions at 200B tokens and 3B parameters, but does not report actual runs at the much larger budgets and model sizes used for its further extrapolations.
No fixed-compute-budget search or test of the loss-minimizing parameter/token split is reported.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count is reported.
The study uses text pretraining; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The scaling analysis evaluates held-out language-model loss, not downstream-task performance or its predictability.

Although results vary by data mixture and scaling axis, the study does not test sensitivity of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation to fitting choices, nor whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: 1B-parameter models (aggregate across six data mixtures)
rows.operation_detail: Fit data-scaling relation using runs up to 100B tokens and validate predictions on 200B-token runs.
rows.measure: Relative Mean Absolute Error (RMABE) of predicted validation loss at 200B tokens
rows.note: The paper reports this aggregate fit-validation error across six mixtures, rather than separate errors for each mixture.
rows.check: Values are correct (0.41% RMABE, six mixtures). For V2 the extrapolation is only 2x: fit to 100B tokens, validated at 200B. This is not orders of magnitude, so the row supports V2 only in that narrow range. The data range of 1B to 200B tokens spans over two orders of magnitude for V1.
